We oppose the design proposal for the following reasons : 1- We Oppose the house being razed and replaced with a sports play yard on the countryside drive address, and therefore having no home on the property. This will negatively impact the view from our street. We also do not want persons parking on our street and walking into this yard’s location and additionally as well , persons accessing the yard with a gate, walkway, or separate entrance of any kind from our street side. Increased traffic will impact the quiet nature of our street and the view will not be a single house dwelling, rather a backyard for the purchasers of the property , and a large fence or green hedge being the view rather than a house. 2- Abiding by rules and regulations of a subdivision have value and purpose. Maintaining these rules and codes of the subdivision allow the neighborhood to remain consistent with its intention. This intention is to have homes occupy the lots and not homeowners changing lot purposes for their own expansions of backyards from opposite streets and changing lot designs for their own purposes of enjoyment. Other homeowners who have invested properly and within the codes maintain these intentions and are concerned when others are allowed to deviate substantially. We ask that Millcreek enforce the existing codes and rules since we will be living the rest of lives on this street with this decision. Your decision will impact our value of our home and the living conditions going forward.

subject: EX-20-004
comment: I would like to appose the exemption being requested. The previous owners of property in question purposefully built an "add-on" to their home with the full intent to use this add-on as an unapproved duplex. These past owners where happy to share this information with neighbors, and thought themselves quite clever. When the property recently came up for sale, the relator was also letting everyone who called know that this was an ILLEGAL duplex. My wife and I called the relator, interested in the sale price, and where told this information before anything else. The new owners of this property where surely also warned about the illegal nature of the property, and choose buy the property with full intent to continue to rent. If you approve this exemption this sets a VERY bad precedent for the community, one where the rules and regulations of the City are blatantly ignored and then manipulated after the fact at the expense of the neighborhood. Duplexes in this area with the current zoning are intended for 2 family units. Instead, at least one of the units is consistently sub- let. While sub-leasing is not the topic of discussion, it has historically attracted individuals who do not participate or interact in the community. The number of sub-letters also often increases to more than 4 individuals, which bypasses the permissible amount. The "MillCreek Together General Plan" for the area in question is listed as a "Neighborhood 1." This type of neighborhood is zoned to be predominately single-family homes. This type of unit does not fit with this plan. This plan also calls for 64% single-family homes and a total of 10% town home, condo, or duplex. From the house in question to 45th south- the number of these (non- single-family homes) is approximately 20%, over double the intended amount. For the neighborhood in general there are over 30% of the homes that are duplexes. Allowing an exemption would not enable the city to maintain the goals listed in the General Plan and maintain the neighborhood as a Neighborhood 1. This property sits at the end of a street that connects to a circle. There is insufficient parking provided for the unsanctioned number of people living at this property, there is insufficient parking. Due to the parking on both sides of the entrance to the circle, there is typically room for one vehicle to enter or exit the circle, not both as is intended, at a time. The renters regularly speed around the circle - turning what should be a safe circle into a dangerous area. With the cars regularly parking on the circle "street" and being that the house in question is at the end of the circle- there is often very cramp conditions when entering or exiting the circle. This parking is due to another infraction—each night 2 to 3 vehicles are parked within the 20 feet of the corner of the circle. It is well documented that on-street parking results in decreased visibility to both pedestrians and vehicles. On-street parking accounts for 72% of all accidents on local streets. The regulations in place to reduce this risk are ignored. Even if the current tenants were different, a corner duplex in this type of neighborhood increases the likelihood of on-street parking, directly increasing the risk for an accident. While an unsafe circle on its own is troubling, it is made even worse in our circle due to the waking path that connects the circle to 45th south. This waking path is intended to improve the safety of access to 4500 South, particularly for pedestrian, cyclists, and access to public transportation. As such, it is regularly trafficked by young families, children, the elderly, as well as special needs individuals from our community. The General Plan encourages walkways and safe walking neighborhoods, and having a duplex on the corner of the road leading to one of these walkways significantly increases the risk of a pedestrian-vehicle accident. While the new owner of this property is surely hoping to turn a quick buck, or bring in a little extra money off this rental, the lasting impacts of the property to those who actually live in the community are not justified by their gain. Neighbors have pervasively filed complaints about the illegal nature of the property. Even the nature and timing of this exemption reflects that, targeting a holiday weekend when many in the community are out of town

subject: Fwd: [Ext] Electronic Billboards
comment: I am a 30+ year resident of the Salt Lake Valley and like many of you I have lived in various parts of the valley throughout those years. On a typical week I spend time in South Salt Lake, Murray, Millcreek, Murray, Riverton and West Jordan as I go about accessing doctor's appointments, my home, my office, shopping, and more. In fact, I drive through Millcreek to get from home to work each day. I am strongly opposed to the addition of electronic billboards in Millcreek that is being discussed tonight. Studies have shown that electronic billboards are more distracting to drivers (I've listed one such study below and tagged the source), and Millcreek is already experiencing increased traffic and the hazards that come with it. While there may be a financial benefit to the city, the potential cost of injury to people and property cannot be overlooked. I hope that the council will reconsider the idea of adding more digital billboards. Maintaining the safety of residents should be the priority. Thank you, Dr. Jen Schwartz, PhD, CFLE -- Third Eye Family Solutions 151 E 5600 South Suite 210 Murray, UT 84107 (385 )347-0805

Hello, I hope this email finds you well. I am writing to urgently bring to your attention a critical matter concerning the safety of our community in Millcreek. It has come to my attention that there is a proposal or ongoing consideration for digital billboards within our city limits. As a concerned resident, I implore you to seriously reconsider this decision due to the significant safety hazards these billboards pose. Digital billboards, while visually intrusive and unsightly, present a far more pressing concern in terms of public safety. Their bright, flashing lights and constantly changing messages serve as an unnecessary distraction to drivers, potentially leading to accidents and endangering lives on our roads. Studies have consistently shown that such distractions contribute to driver fatigue, decreased reaction times, and an increased likelihood of accidents. Millcreek prides itself on being a safe and welcoming community for all residents and visitors. Introducing more digital billboards contradicts this commitment and puts our citizens at unnecessary risk. Moreover, these billboards detract from the aesthetic appeal of our neighborhoods and commercial areas, diminishing the overall quality of life for those who call Millcreek home. As our elected representative on the planning commission, I urge you to take swift and decisive action to prevent the installation or expansion of digital billboards in our city. It is imperative that we prioritize the safety and well-being of our community above all else. I implore you to consider the long-term ramifications of allowing such structures to proliferate in Millcreek and to act in the best interests of those you serve. Please do not hesitate to reach out to me if you require any further information or if there are additional steps I can take to support this urgent matter. The safety of our community depends on our collective action and responsibility. Thank you for your prompt attention to this pressing issue.

Dear Planning Commission, My husband and I have been residents in Lexington Village in Old Farm for over 10 years. We have been told that we can submit comments and concerns to the planning commission for consideration. I was out of town and unable to attend the Open House on May 5, however, I have spoken with several others who did attend and have obtained some of the information that was available, mainly the floor plans and the site plan. Here are the points I hope the committee will consider: 1. It seems premature to have this project before the planning commission when there are still a number of unknowns. In looking at the site plan, it appears it has not been updated with the latest floor plans, particularly the new ‘porches’ that have been added to the structures. I am particularly concerned about the three proposed units on the west side of the property. It looks like there is no setback from the current right of way that exists between the main parcel and the unbuildable parcel by the pond. And yet, it looks like there is a ‘patio’ added to the west side of structures D, E and F. Since there are no measurements on the floor plans, I can’t tell how far out that reaches but it is unclear how the developer proposes to accommodate that addition. 2. The site plan shows the above-mentioned right of way as a sidewalk instead of the current roadway that exists. I have been told they plan to keep it as a gravel roadway but that should be reflected on the site plan. 3. My biggest concern is about the proposed height of the structures. Apparently, at the open house the developer would not commit to what that height will be, only saying they can be ‘up to 32 feet’. Earlier in this process, when the HOA took the first vote for allowing the project to join the HOA, they stated that the one and half story units would be 26 feet high. I’m not sure why there are no heights on the floor plan documents, but it would seem that should be decided at this point and another reason why this is premature. 4. I object to these units being called ‘ramblers’ because they are, in fact, two-story units. The livable space on the upper floor consists of a bedroom, full bathroom, two closets, one large storage area, and a ‘loft’ open space. The square footage appears to be similar to the square footage in the basement. Especially if the height of the buildings will be anywhere close to 32 feet, it is a two-story unit. Although it is 1 difficult to tell because there appears to be no square footage measurements on the plans or I cannot tell how to read that. 5. All of the other buildings in Lexington Village are true ‘ramblers’ with finished square footage above the first floor. The current maximum heights of the existing units is 18 feet at the peak of some of the garages, but more like 15 feet at the peak of the existing main buildings. The proposed units will TOWER over the existing units at around twice the height and will not blend in with the existing units. 6. It’s my understanding that true one-story units do ‘not pencil out’ for the developer and why they are forced to go up and develop more finished square footage. 7. In my opinion, the size of the land parcel does not support the development of these large units. If you take away the unbuildable portion of the parcel by the pond, the density of the units and especially with the height will feel very crowded and again, not consistent with the existing units. 8. I have also heard comments that the developer is planning to move the entire project some number of feet to the south, however, this is not reflected anywhere on the site plan. It is important for the residents to understand what exactly is being proposed. Again, why this action is premature. 9. I am concerned about the number of mature trees that will be removed to accommodate this project. The trees and landscaping are what lends the ambience and character of Lexington Village. I have a dog that I walk 3-4 times a day around the property and enjoy the landscaping, trees, grass, and open space and fear this new development will destroy the existing feeling and views, especially along the pond. The Lexington Village HOA will hold another vote once all of the final dimensions, square footage, height, and all of the agreements between the developer and the HOA are finalized. If the developer keeps changing previous commitments it may be that more of the owners will change their mind about allowing them into the HOA. Please consider these items as the development goes through the planning process with Millcreek City.

Dear Mr. Murray, Here are my comments regarding the project as presented at the open house by the developer, Matt Knight, and some background information. I live in Lexington Village and have owned a condo there for over 22 years. My husband and I bought a condo there because of the open common areas, pond, the ambience, and its rich history. My husband was an architectural historian. All of the condos in Lexington Village are one-story, except for one brick two-story house that is original to the property. That house is well-hidden by trees and faces Old Farm Road, not Old Farm Way. The planned development does not consist of one-story condos. The developer at the meeting, and at prior times when he has discussed the project with Lexington Village HOA members, refers to the condos as ramblers. They are not ramblers. They are huge one and a half story structures that according to the developer will be 32-feet tall or possibly some might be a couple of feet shorter. He was very vague about the height, but he did have elevations that did not include measurements. When asked about the square footage, he said six of the condos would be around 3,000 square feet and the three closest to the pond would be around 3,500 square feet and then he changed it to maybe around 4,000 square feet. Again, he gave vague answers. Since it was an open house regarding the project, I would’ve expected him to be better prepared. On prior occasions when the developer met with Lexington Village HOA members, he said the condos would be 26 feet tall. Even at that height, they would be appreciably taller than the 3 Sean Murray, planner Page 2 May 6, 2026 current condos, which are 15 feet at the roof peak located at the side of the buildings. So, the front of the condos is much shorter. The manor house units do have garages that are 18 feet at the peak, but they can’t be seen from the road or sidewalks. You can only see the garages if you drive down one of the driveways. The planned condos don’t fit in with Lexington Village condos. All of the current 77 condos have private courtyards. They don’t exist in the proposed project. The private outdoor space per unit in the project is minimal because the condos, roads and sidewalks fill most of the buildable area in the .94 acre property. The 32-foot condos would tower over all 77 existing condos, disrupting the neighborhood’s scale and overwhelming the low profile of the current community. They will also have a significant impact on the ambience, character, and Lexington Village’s deep-rooted history. The Lexington Village HOA did have a preliminary vote whether or not to allow the project in our HOA. It did receive the required 2/3rd yes votes, but the members were not voting on the design. The Lexington Village owners that I talked to, which was a significant number, who voted “yes” did it because of the following concerns: the units could turn into rental properties, possibly become Air B and B’s, and we could not police the new buyers from parking on our private street, in guest parking areas, or enjoying our common areas and they wouldn’t be paying dues for the maintenance. Having them in the HOA would give the HOA control over those concerns and the buyers would be paying dues. In closing, please take into consideration that every condo in Lexington Village is a single story. The introduction of 32-foot structures would stand out dramatically, dominating the skyline and overshadowing the surrounding condos. And Lexington Village is unique, no other condominiums in Millcreek have a park-like setting, a pond, and a storied history.
